meta.title: The potential adverse effects of hypodermic glucagon-like peptide -1 receptor agonist on patients with type 2 diabetes: A population-based study.
meta.abstract:
Background

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), a class of injectable antidiabetic drugs, have shown significant efficacies in improving glycemic and weight control in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the long-term safety of GLP-1 RAs remains insufficiently studied. This study aimed to provide real-world evidence on potential adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use in T2D patients without major chronic diseases including impaired cardiac or renal function.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 7746 T2D patients on GLP-1 RAs in Shenzhen, China. They were compared with 124 371 metformin-only users and 36 146 insulin-only users, forming two therapy control groups. GLP-1 RAs users were also further 1:2 paired with the control groups. Competing risk survival analyses were conducted to assess the incidence risks, presenting subdistributional hazard ratios (sHRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for various adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use.

Results

Compared with metformin-only users, GLP-1 RAs use was associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes (sHRs with 95% CIs), including pancreatitis (2.01, 1.24-3.24), acute nephritis (3.20, 2.17-4.70), kidney failure (3.73, 2.74-5.08), thyroid cancer (2.25, 1.23-4.10), and thyroid dysfunction (1.27, 1.00-1.63), respectively; Similar results were also found when compared with insulin-only users. Importantly, long-term (≥12 months) GLP-1 RAs use may further elevate the incidence risks of pancreatitis, acute nephritis, thyroid cancer, and thyroid dysfunction.

Conclusion

Compared with traditional T2D treatments, GLP-1 RAs use may be associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes in a Chinese population. Cautions were strongly warranted in the use of GLP-1 RAs. Further validation is crucial across diverse populations.

domains.name: Confounding
domains.direction_justification: GLP-1 RA users had higher baseline BMI (BMI 30.0-39.9: 13.21% vs 4.87% in metformin and 3.04% in insulin) and higher socioeconomic/insurance status. Critical confounders like HbA1c were missing in 90.52% to 91.79% of patients and FPG in 24.13% to 32.95%, preventing control for diabetes severity. Confounding by indication and residual confounding likely inflated risk estimates across unrelated outcomes (e.g., leukemia sHR 15.09, 95% CI: 4.65–48.98; renal failure sHR 3.73, 95% CI: 2.74–5.08).

domains.name: Selection of participants into the study
domains.direction_justification: Massive attrition during cohort construction (177,381 excluded for missing IDs, 362,035 excluded for missing prescription data out of 985,278 total outpatients) creates potential selection bias with unknown directional effect on risk estimates.

findings.title: Massive patient exclusions due to missing database identifiers and records
findings.mechanism: Excluding over 54% of the target outpatient population (177,381 missing ID, 362,035 missing prescription data) can induce collider stratification and selection bias if data completeness correlates with health status or healthcare utilization.
evidence: Initial outpatient diabetes population: 985,278; excluded for missing ID: 177,381; excluded for missing prescription: 362,035; eligible cohort: 380,370 (Figure 1)

findings.title: Immortal time / conditioning on future exposure pattern
findings.mechanism: Exposure classification required cumulative antidiabetic prescription patterns from baseline to the last follow-up date, potentially conditioning on post-baseline survival and continuous care.
evidence: Definition required cumulative diabetes prescription primarily consistent of GLP-1 RAs, insulin, or metformin lasting from baseline date to last follow-up date

domains.name: Post-exposure interventions
domains.direction_justification: Competing risk survival models (subdistribution HRs) were implemented to account for treatment interruptions/discontinuations triggered by acute side effects.

findings.title: Competing risk framework applied for treatment-related discontinuations
findings.mechanism: Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard models were used treating acute side effect occurrences as competing risks.
evidence: Systematic binomial competing events defined by acute side effects (diarrhea, dizziness, arrhythmia, etc.) using sub-distribution hazard ratios (sHRs)

domains.name: Missing data
domains.direction_justification: Missingness exceeding 90% for primary clinical indicators (HbA1c) and 24-34% for BMI and FPG was handled by creating 'unspecified' indicator bins rather than multiple imputation or complete case analysis, allowing unmeasured baseline disease severity to confound effect estimates away from the null.

findings.title: Extreme missingness in core metabolic severity markers
findings.mechanism: Matching on missingness indicators ('unspecified') leaves unaddressed substantial residual differences within the missing categories.
evidence: HbA1c missing rate: 90.52% (GLP-1 RAs), 91.79% (insulin), 90.45% (metformin)
FPG missing rate: 32.95% (GLP-1 RAs), 32.66% (insulin), 24.13% (metformin)
BMI missing rate: 32.31% (GLP-1 RAs), 32.78% (insulin), 24.01% (metformin)

domains.name: Measurement of the outcome
domains.direction_justification: Detection and surveillance bias: Patients on injectable GLP-1 RAs, especially those paying privately or with higher socioeconomic status (26.07% undergraduate+ vs 11.94% in metformin), undergo closer clinical monitoring, laboratory workups, and ultrasound/imaging, increasing incidental detection of subclinical thyroid disorders and kidney abnormalities.

findings.title: Surveillance and diagnostic workup bias
findings.mechanism: GLP-1 RA initiation involves gastrointestinal symptoms leading to frequent laboratory and imaging workups, inflating diagnoses of acute nephritis, pancreatitis, and thyroid nodules/cancer.
evidence: Outcomes identified through unadjudicated ICD-10 codes and regex matching in outpatient/inpatient electronic medical records (Table 2S)
GLP-1 RA cohort had higher education (26.07% vs 11.94% undergraduate+) and citizen health insurance coverage (75.60% vs 54.96%) vs metformin (Table 3S)

domains.name: Selection of the reported result
domains.direction_justification: Testing dozens of unadjudicated disease categories across multiple subgroups and exposure durations without multi-testing correction inflates the likelihood of spurious statistically significant findings (e.g., leukemia sHR 15.09, acne sHR 5.32).

findings.title: Multiple outcome testing without multiplicity correction
findings.mechanism: Evaluating multiple ICD-10 disease categories across stratified exposure durations (<12 months, >=12 months) and individual drug agents increases type I error.
evidence: Over 18 individual clinical outcomes tested simultaneously across multiple comparison groups and drug subclasses at alpha = 0.05

overall.summary: This retrospective cohort study reports elevated risks for numerous adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RA use compared with insulin and metformin monotherapies. However, the study is at very high risk of bias due to extreme missingness of critical confounding variables (>90% missing HbA1c, ~33% missing BMI/FPG), matching on 'unspecified' missing categories, massive participant exclusion (>50% excluded due to missing IDs or prescription data), and substantial diagnostic surveillance bias among GLP-1 RA users. Implausibly large effect sizes across biologically unrelated outcomes (such as leukemia sHR 15.09 and acne sHR 5.32) strongly indicate pervasive residual confounding by indication, surveillance bias, and statistical noise rather than true causal drug effects.

unresolvable_without_more_data: Raw event numbers and person-time per arm for individual adverse outcomes are not provided in the text or supplementary tables, precluding independent calculation of absolute risk differences and incidence rates.
True baseline glycemic control and diabetes duration/severity data for the >90% of patients with missing HbA1c to evaluate residual confounding by indication.

baseline_comparability.summary: Baseline imbalances before matching showed GLP-1 RA users were younger but substantially more obese, more educated, and more extensively insured than comparator groups, with severe baseline data missingness (>90% for HbA1c). These imbalances in obesity and healthcare access favour elevated outcome detection in the GLP-1 RA group, pushing risk estimates away from the null.

time_related_biases.summary: The study defines exposure groups retrospectively across total follow-up rather than at treatment initiation and applies no lag period for slow-latency outcomes like thyroid cancer. These temporal misalignments introduce immortal time bias and surveillance/protopathic bias, driving risk estimates away from the null.
